questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following:

(i) Barter system of trade. (2 marks)
(ii) Inflation. (2 marks)
(iii) Price index. (2 marks)
(iv) Credit creation. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Barter system of trade.** Barter is the **direct exchange of goods and services for other goods and services, without the use of money**. For example, a farmer exchanges a bag of maize for a pair of sandals. It requires a *double coincidence of wants* (each person must want what the other has).

**(ii) Inflation.** Inflation is a **persistent (sustained) rise in the general level of prices** over a period of time, so that the purchasing power of money falls: the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services.

**(iii) Price index.** A price index is a **statistical measure of the average change in the prices of a basket of goods and services over time compared with a base year**, whose index is fixed at 100:

$$
\text{Price index}=\frac{\text{cost of the basket in the current year}}{\text{cost of the basket in the base year}}\times 100
$$

Example (hypothetical): if the basket costs 20,000 FCFA in the base year and 23,000 FCFA this year, the index is $\frac{23\,000}{20\,000}\times100=115$, so prices have risen by 15% on average.

**(iv) Credit creation.** Credit creation is the process by which **commercial banks create new deposits (money) by lending**. Since customers do not all withdraw their money at the same time, a bank keeps only a fraction of deposits as cash reserve and lends the rest; the amount lent is spent and deposited again in a bank, which lends part of it, and so on, so that total deposits become a multiple of the original cash.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below are some functions of financial institutions in our economy.

(i) Lending to members of the public.
(ii) Lending to commercial banks.
(iii) Agent of payment to customers.
(iv) Agent of payment to the state.

Which of these functions best explain the activity of commercial and central banks in your Country? (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Function | Institution | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| (i) Lending to members of the public | **Commercial banks** | They grant loans and overdrafts to individuals and businesses, which is their main source of profit |
| (ii) Lending to commercial banks | **Central bank** | It is the "bankers' bank" and lender of last resort: it lends to commercial banks that are short of cash |
| (iii) Agent of payment to customers | **Commercial banks** | They pay their customers' cheques, transfers and cash withdrawals and make standing-order payments for them |
| (iv) Agent of payment to the state | **Central bank** | It is the government's banker: it receives government revenue and makes payments on the government's behalf |

In Cameroon, the central bank is the regional central bank of the CEMAC member countries (the Bank of Central African States, BEAC), while commercial banks are the ordinary banks that serve households and firms.

questions.enonce_markdown: State and explain FOUR (4) limitations of commercial banks to create credit. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Commercial banks create credit by lending more than the cash they hold, but they cannot create it without limit. The main limitations are as follows.

1. **The cash (reserve) ratio.** A bank must keep a minimum proportion of its deposits in cash or at the central bank to meet withdrawals. The higher this ratio, the less it can lend. For example (hypothetical), with a 10% cash ratio, an initial cash deposit of 1,000,000 FCFA can support total deposits of at most $\frac{1\,000\,000}{0.10}=10\,000\,000$ FCFA, that is, new credit of $10\,000\,000-1\,000\,000=9\,000\,000$ FCFA.
2. **The amount of cash deposits available.** Credit is built on the cash base: if customers deposit little cash (or the central bank supplies little cash to the banks), the banks have less to lend.
3. **Control by the central bank.** The central bank can restrict credit by raising the rate at which it lends to banks or the required reserve ratio, by selling securities to take cash out of the banking system, and by giving directives or credit ceilings.
4. **The demand for loans and the shortage of credit-worthy borrowers.** Banks lend only to borrowers who can repay and offer security. If interest rates are high or businessmen are not confident about the future, few people ask for loans, so credit cannot expand.

*Other limitations:* a habit of holding cash instead of using bank accounts (cash drain), and the banks' need to remain liquid so as to avoid a run on the bank.

**Conclusion.** These limitations protect depositors and help the central bank to control the money supply.
